Thirteen-year-old Dakota had been missing for three days in the sweltering July heat
when a specialist arrived to help the poor boy. This was no ordinary rescuer; it was Scout a
six-year-old bloodhound from the Farmington K-9 unit. For Scout tracking is a routine: he gets
into his gear, relaxes for a moment, and then waits for a co-worker to present a scent. On this
blazing afternoon, the stakes were incredibly high.
The ordeal began on Sunday, July 27, 2025. Dakota had set off across his grandmother's
home in Goose Creek Lake, on his grey skateboard. Security cameras captured him skating past
a firehouse around 9 a.m., wearing a Harry Potter T-shirt, and a ball cap. Dakota usually carried
a school backpack when visiting his friend. However, on the tragic day, he was not carrying it.
It was a route he took daily to visit his friend, Sam but Dakota never arrived
When he failed to return by his usual 4 p.m. deadline, his grandmother became anxious.
Since Dakota did not have his mobile phone, she contacted Sam, only to discover that Dakota
had been missing all day. Panic soon set in for Dakota's mother, Stephanie, a corrections officer.
While authorities initially suspected the teenager might have run away, Stephanie was certain
something was wrong. Her son was a creature of habit, and disappearing without a call or text
was completely out of character.
The search intensified. A team of nearly 50 volunteers, including Dakota's aunt
Brittney—a volunteer firefighter—conducted a meticulous grid search. They utilized all-terrain
vehicles and motorcycles, but the dense, wooded ravines of the 2,500-acre development proved
difficult to navigate. As days passed, Stephanie struggled to remain optimistic, aware of the
grim statistics regarding missing persons after 72 hours.
The breakthrough occurred on Wednesday morning. Dakota's brother, Steven, spotted a
familiar grey skateboard lying in tall grass near a steep ravine. The board's position was
chilling-the front end pointed down into a deep, rocky incline. Stephanie and her husband
attempted to descend, but the terrain was treacherous and slick from recent rain. They could not
find any footsteps, which made them fear that something bad had happened
The local sheriff's department realised their own K-9 units, primarily German
shepherds, were not suited for a trail this cold. They requested Scout the bloodhound known for
his ability to track older scents in thick vegetation. When Scout's handler, Lt. Joe Gillam,
arrived, he offered no guarantees. Tracking a three-day-old scent was a challenge as it had
become difficult to follow.
Within minutes, the dog signaled he had picked up a scent.
"He's got something!" one of the rescuers shouted.
Scout led the team down a 15-foot drop into the ravine. The rescuers followed him
through thick oak trees and heavy undergrowth. Shortly into the search, they discovered
Dakota's discarded T-shirt and trousers. Twenty-one minutes after starting, the radio crackled
with a visual confirmation.
"I found him! He's alive!" a rescuer yelled
Dakota was found lying in a shallow, temporary creek created by the rain. While the
water had likely saved him from overheating in the July sun, he was severely dehydrated and
unable to speak. A member of the K-9 unit carefully administered water drop by drop. Against
all odds, Dakota was alive.

We interviewed six students about how they can help the environment. Read the texts below and
answer the questions that follow:
A- Azizah, 16 years old
Instead of buying 'fast fashion' clothes, I spend my weekends thrifting at bundle shops or
organising clothing swaps with my friends. It is fun because I have to mix and match
unique pieces to create my own style. Not only do I save money, but 1 also help reduce
water and energy used in textile production.
B- Bavithrah, 17 years old
I now cycle, use public transport, or share car rides for my daily commute. It can be quite
tiring in the heat, but it is a great way to stay fit. By avoiding car rides, 1 am directly
lowering the carbon footprints in my residential area and reducing traffic congestion.
C- Chloe, 15 years old
I am the "Energy Monitor" in my household and ensure that all electrical appliances and
lights are switched off when a room is not in use. I also remind my siblings to unplug
their phone chargers once they reach 100% as it reduces our monthly household expenses.
Most importantly, using less electricity means less coal is burned to produce electricity.
D - Dani, 19 years old
I am a culinary student, and started a small composting project in my backyard. I collect
fruit peels and vegetable scraps from the kitchen instead of throwing them into the trash.
It is fascinating to see how waste turns into rich soil! This prevents organic waste from
releasing methane gas in landfills and provides free compost for my mom's garden.
E -Esther, 18 years old
I hate seeing how many plastic cups and straws being thrown every week. Now, I always
carry my own tumblers and metal straws in my bag. Now, many cafes even give me a
small discount for bringing my own cup. It feels good knowing I am not contributing to
the plastic pollution in our oceans.
F - Fei Hong, 14 years old
I learn that the meat industry contributes a lot to greenhouse gas emissions. Once a week,
I take over the kitchen and prepare plant-based meals, like lentil soup or veggie burgers.
It is a fun way to experiment with new recipes.It helps my family eat healthier while
saving the environment.
